summary: This standards-track RFC defines HTTP status code 451, which a server can use to say that access to a resource is denied because of a legal demand, such as a court order or government request. It lets clients and users tell legal blocking apart from ordinary errors like 403 Forbidden.

eli5.summary: When a website is blocked because a law or a judge says so, it can now say that clearly with its own special error number, instead of pretending something else went wrong.

questions: http status code for legal blocking
what does 451 unavailable for legal reasons mean
what is the blocked-by link relation
subtitle: HTTP status 451 lets a server say a page is blocked because of a legal demand.

tldr.problem: When access to a resource is denied because of a legal demand, existing codes such as 403 do not say so, and users cannot tell legal blocking from other failures.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines status code 451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons, asks for an explanatory body, and defines a blocked-by link relation to identify the blocking entity.
tldr.outcome: Legal blocking can be made explicit, but clients cannot rely on it because some authorities may want to avoid transparency.

today: RFC 7725 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why a Legal-Reasons Code
sections.content:
This RFC specifies an HTTP status code for use when a server operator has received a legal demand to deny access to a resource, or to a set of resources that includes the requested one. It can provide transparency where law or public policy affects server operations, which may help both operators and end users.

It builds on RFC 4924, which discusses forces working against transparent operation of the Internet, and on RFC 4084, which says such restrictions should be made explicit. The thanks section credits the observation that status 403 was not really suitable.
sections.eli5: When a door is locked because of a rule, it helps to have a sign that says so, not just a plain "no".

sections.title: 451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons
sections.content:
The code 451 means the server is denying access as a consequence of a legal demand. The server might not be an origin server; such demands typically affect ISPs and search engines most directly.

Responses SHOULD include an explanation in the body of the details: the party making the demand, the applicable legislation or regulation, and what classes of person and resource it applies to. The code implies neither the existence nor nonexistence of the resource. A 451 response is cacheable by default. The RFC notes that clients can often still reach the content using technical countermeasures such as a VPN or the Tor network.
sections.eli5: The sign should say who ordered the lock and which rule it comes from, though it does not say whether anything is behind the door.

sections.title: Identifying the Blocking Entity
sections.content:
The entity that blocks access might be an ISP, cache provider or DNS server rather than the origin server. When an entity blocks a resource and returns 451, it SHOULD include a Link header field whose value is a URI reference identifying itself, with a rel parameter of blocked-by.

The header should identify the entity actually implementing the blockage, not any other entity mandating it. Discussion of administrative and policy issues belongs in the human-readable body.
sections.eli5: The sign should also name who put up the lock, not who gave the order.

sections.title: Limits and Registrations
sections.content:
Clients cannot rely on the 451 code. Some legal authorities might demand restricted access and also avoid disclosing that the demand was made.

IANA added 451 (Unavailable For Legal Reasons) to the HTTP Status Codes Registry and the blocked-by relation to the Link Relation Type Registry.
sections.eli5: Someone might order the lock and also order that there be no sign, so a missing sign does not prove there is no rule.

data.title: 451 response
data.code:
HTTP/1.1 451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons
Link: <https://spqr.example.org/legislatione>; rel="blocked-by"
Content-Type: text/html
